clue.text: Tense situation for an abseiling enthusiast

definitions.meaning: a story or contest left in suspense, its outcome unknown until the last moment
someone who likes dangling on a rope from a rock face, read literally as one who hangs from cliffs

explanation.surface: A climber who loves abseiling finds themselves in a nerve-racking spot.
explanation.definitionFit: The suspenseful sense is the idiom for a gripping unresolved ending; the second is a jokey literal coinage for a person dangling from rock.

clue.text: See airman in the neighbourhood

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'See airman in the neighbourhood': LO for 'See' leaves CAL, which no usual sense of 'airman' gives (AC is the convention), so a word appears to be missing or misread and no scan is available

clue.text: Supervisor runs into an enemy

indicators.note: the word for runs goes into the middle of the word for an enemy

parts.note: a foeman is an old word for an enemy in battle
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A boss charges headlong at an adversary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'runs' reads as a verb, someone charging into a foe, but it is the cricket abbreviation; 'into' puts it inside the old word for an enemy.
explanation.definitionFit: A works manager or chief of a jury is one who oversees others, a supervisor.

clue.text: Stores vast numbers, by the sound of it

indicators.note: this phrase tells us the letters are those of a word that is pronounced like the one meant

parts.note: hordes are huge crowds or swarms

explanation.surface: A warehouse holds enormous quantities, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stores vast numbers' reads as one statement, but 'Stores' is the definition and 'vast numbers' the word heard.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to stockpile or keep secret reserves is to put by supplies, which matches 'stores'.

clue.text: A month before Fitzgerald's stories appear

parts.note: Nov is the short form of November
Ella Fitzgerald, the jazz singer, plus the possessive S

explanation.surface: F. Scott Fitzgerald's stories come out a month early.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the novelist F. Scott Fitzgerald, but the Fitzgerald meant is the singer Ella.
explanation.definitionFit: Short novels are works of fiction, tales longer than a short story.

clue.text: Former nobleman introduced to King Edward

annotationWithheld.clue: Former nobleman introduced to King Edward

clue.text: Also censoring resolution of the US legislature

indicators.note: a resolution here is a working out or breaking down, so the letters of the phrase are rearranged

explanation.surface: Censorship is another resolution passed by lawmakers in Washington.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resolution' looks like a motion passed by a legislature but signals the anagram of ALSO CENSORING.
explanation.definitionFit: Congress is the federal legislature of the United States, so this adjective describes its business.

clue.text: Security services inflamed by worker from Trotskyite group

parts.note: MI, Military Intelligence, as in MI5 and MI6, the British security services
set on fire, lit
the worker ant is the crossword's stock worker

explanation.surface: Spies stirred up by an activist from a far-left faction.
explanation.walkthrough: Militant was a Trotskyist faction inside the British Labour Party in the 1980s.
explanation.definitionFit: The Militant Tendency was the name of a far-left entryist organisation within the Labour Party.

clue.text: Going blind taking mortality count

parts.note: being mortal ends in being dead
a reckoning is a calculation or tally

explanation.surface: A census of deaths is taken while one loses one's sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going blind' sounds like losing sight; it means navigating without instruments, by calculation alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Navigators estimate position from speed, heading and time when they cannot see landmarks or stars.

clue.text: Large limousine gains Academy Award

parts.note: OS stands for outsize, a clothing label for large
a limousine is a kind of car

explanation.surface: A stretch limo carries off a film award.
explanation.definitionFit: The statuette given by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences is known by this nickname.

clue.text: Bill is hostile about returning it

indicators.note: the word for hostile is placed around the other piece

parts.note: adverse means opposed or unfavourable

indicators.note: this word tells us the little word it is read backwards

explanation.surface: An invoice is unwelcome when it comes back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a noun but is the verb: to bill a show is to promote it. 'returning' turns only 'it', and 'about' wraps the hostile word around that.
explanation.definitionFit: To bill a performance is to announce or promote it publicly on posters.

clue.text: Fashion model glad to win first prize

indicators.note: used as a verb, to fashion is to shape, so the letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: A catwalk model is delighted to come top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fashion' poses as the catwalk world but is a verb telling us to reshape MODEL GLAD.
explanation.definitionFit: Winners of Olympic and other competitions receive this award for coming top.

clue.text: Long poem initially inscribed 1942 years ago

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the word inscribed is taken

parts.note: counted back from the puzzle's publication in 1993 the year is AD 51, written in Roman numerals LI and the era AD

explanation.surface: An epic first carved in stone almost two millennia back.
explanation.walkthrough: The puzzle dates from 1993, so 1942 years earlier is AD 51: LI is 51 in Roman numerals, followed by AD.
explanation.definitionFit: Homer's epic of the Trojan War runs to twenty-four books, a lengthy verse narrative.

clue.text: Making a mistake by hesitation to call

parts.note: er is the sound of hesitating in speech
to ring someone is to telephone them

explanation.surface: Dithering before phoning turns out to be an error.
explanation.definitionFit: To err is to go astray or slip up, so this participle means getting something wrong.

clue.text: Era of violence requires real fibre

parts.note: rough treatment is violence
an era is an age

explanation.surface: A violent period demands genuine moral fibre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fibre' suggests strength of character; it is dietary fibre. The pieces run 'violence' then 'Era', as in a rough age.
explanation.definitionFit: Bran and coarse vegetable matter form the indigestible bulk in food that aids digestion.

clue.text: One rightly ridiculed hoop-la, for instance

definitions.meaning: a person who can justly be mocked or attacked
hoop-la is a sideshow at a funfair where rings are thrown over prizes

explanation.surface: A deserved butt of jokes, like a ring-tossing stall.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a legitimate target of criticism; literally, it is any stall amusement played at a funfair.

clue.text: Single issue leading to anti-government agitation

indicators.note: the first piece goes in front of the second

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for single, as on forms giving marital status
an issue of a newspaper is an edition

explanation.surface: A one-issue campaign stirring up revolt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Single issue' reads as a political campaign, but splits into S and EDITION.
explanation.definitionFit: Speech or conduct inciting rebellion against the state is a criminal offence of incitement.

clue.text: Australian sheep-farmer is comparatively short and fat

definitions.meaning: in Australia, a large-scale grazier who first occupied crown land
the comparative of squat, meaning stocky

explanation.surface: An Aussie rancher is stockier than most.
explanation.walkthrough: In Australian usage the word named a settler who took up crown land for grazing, later a wealthy pastoralist.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the Australian term for a big landholder of sheep runs; the other is the comparative of stocky.

clue.text: Dull seaman getting up in silence

parts.note: tar is old slang for a sailor

indicators.note: in a down clue, getting up means the word in is read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: sh is the call for silence

explanation.surface: A tedious sailor rising quietly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dull' looks like an adjective describing the seaman, but it is the verb. 'getting up' turns IN into NI, going up the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: To tarnish metal is to make it lose its shine, to dull it.

clue.text: Composer expresses approval of a knight

parts.note: Bart is the abbreviation for baronet, a hereditary title ranking just above a knight
OK signals approval

explanation.surface: A musician voices his endorsement of a titled gentleman.
explanation.walkthrough: Béla Bartók was a Hungarian composer. A baronet is not strictly a knight, but the title carries 'Sir', which is the setter's licence.
explanation.definitionFit: Béla Bartók was a twentieth-century Hungarian writer of music, known for string quartets and folk-influenced works.

clue.text: Leave with one's hair tied back?

parts.note: one, as A, with the possessive giving no letter
hair tied back is held by a band
with in the sense of wearing, having it on

explanation.surface: Departing with a ponytail?
explanation.walkthrough: Read the definition's partner as 'a band on': someone with hair tied back has a band on. The question mark flags that whimsy.
explanation.definitionFit: To desert or give up a place or person is to quit it, to go away for good.

clue.text: Man in the middle has to be consistent

indicators.note: the word for man goes inside the word for middle

parts.note: the core is the centre
he is a male person

explanation.surface: A man caught between two sides must stay steady.
explanation.definitionFit: To stick together logically, as an argument whose parts fit, is to hang together.

clue.text: Additional article carried by ordinary soldiers

indicators.note: the article is held inside the letters for the soldiers

parts.note: OR, ... ranks, the enlisted soldiers below officers
the is the definite article

explanation.surface: A further piece of kit borne by the troops.
explanation.walkthrough: OR (other ranks) is the British Army term for soldiers who are not officers.
explanation.definitionFit: Something further or extra beyond what is already mentioned is more, another.

clue.text: An oil is to be blended in a place apart

indicators.note: blending mixes things, so these letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: Oil is mixed in to make something set apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' belongs to the fodder: AN OIL IS TO has the nine letters needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Being set apart from others, as in quarantine or a remote spot, is solitude or separation.

clue.text: To sleep in it is not appropriate

indicators.note: the word for sleeping goes inside the little word it

parts.note: to nap is to doze briefly

explanation.surface: Dozing off on the job is unsuitable.
explanation.definitionFit: Unsuitable or ill-fitting remarks are inappropriate or unfitting.

clue.text: Make English ceilings a different way

indicators.note: doing it a different way means these letters are arranged afresh

explanation.surface: An instruction to build ceilings in the English style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a' joins the fodder: CEILINGS plus A gives the nine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To adapt foreign words or customs to the style of England is to anglify them.

clue.text: Depicted with gaunt features

definitions.meaning: pictured in pencil or ink, sketched
haggard or tired-looking in the face

explanation.surface: Sketched showing a haggard face.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the past participle of sketch-making; the other describes a face pinched by fatigue or worry.

clue.text: Alter a chit to get some silver

definitions.meaning: to amend a memo or short written message
to swap a banknote for coins, silver being coins

explanation.surface: Amend an IOU to get some cash.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both amending a written message and exchanging a banknote for coins.
